content.markdown: Shelfwise is a TypeScript service that manages warehouse stock and order reservations. It includes a small admin front end and handles up to 3,000 reservations per hour.

content.markdown: This tour organizes the code by responsibility, detailing module ownership, key files, and inter-group dependencies. The main groups are:

- Presentation
- API and orchestration
- Domain services
- Supplier integration
- Persistence and external systems
- Observability and error handling

content.markdown: Shelfwise is the service that keeps track of how much stock each warehouse holds and reserves stock for incoming orders. This tour walks through the code by responsibility: what each group of modules owns, which files to open first, and how the groups depend on each other.

Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Client and presentation ⨁ Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › API and orchestration ⨁ Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase~9e6a3843~tory service: a tour of the codebase › Observability and error handling § text#0

content.markdown: The admin web UI lives in `web/admin/`. Warehouse staff use it to look up stock levels, place manual holds and review failed supplier imports. It holds no stock logic of its own: every screen calls the service's REST API, and the UI never talks to the database directly.

nodes.stableKey: Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Client and presentation ⨁ Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › API and orchestration ⨁ Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase~ec3a9970~ory service: a tour of the codebase › Observability and error handling § shape#1

Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Client and presentation ⨁ Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › API and orchestration ⨁ Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase~9d6a36b0~tory service: a tour of the codebase › Observability and error handling § text#1

content.markdown:
The HTTP handlers in `src/api/routes.ts` are the only entry point for requests. They validate the request body, attach a correlation ID and pass the work on; they contain no business rules. A `POST /reservations` request goes to the reservation orchestrator in `src/orders/reserve.ts`.

The reservation orchestrator coordinates a reservation from start to finish. It asks the stock ledger to reserve the requested quantity, asks the pricing rules for the order's price, and, once both succeed, publishes a StockReserved event to the message broker. If the ledger cannot reserve the full quantity, the orchestrator rejects the whole order; it never makes a partial reservation. A reservation that is not confirmed within 15 minutes is released by the ledger and the stock becomes available again.

nodes.stableKey: Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Client and presentation ⨁ Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › API and orchestration ⨁ Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase~ef3a9e29~ory service: a tour of the codebase › Observability and error handling § shape#2

Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Client and presentation ⨁ Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › API and orchestration ⨁ Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase~9f6a39d6~tory service: a tour of the codebase › Observability and error handling § text#3

content.markdown:
The stock ledger in `src/ledger/ledger.ts` owns stock levels. It records every change as an append-only ledger entry (reserve, release, restock) and writes those entries to Postgres. The ledger is the only module allowed to write to the stock tables; other modules ask it to make changes.

The pricing rules in `src/pricing/rules.ts` work out the price of an order from the supplier price lists and any active discounts. They read price lists from Redis, where they are cached for 300 seconds, and they never change stock.

Neither domain module imports anything from `src/api/` or `src/orders/`. Dependencies point inwards: the API layer calls the orchestrator, the orchestrator calls the domain modules, and the domain modules depend only on persistence and the platform helpers.

nodes.stableKey: Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Client and presentation ⨁ Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › API and orchestration ⨁ Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase~ee3a9c96~ory service: a tour of the codebase › Observability and error handling § shape#3

Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Client and presentation ⨁ Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › API and orchestration ⨁ Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase~a46a41b5~tory service: a tour of the codebase › Observability and error handling § text#6

content.markdown: The supplier feed adapter in `src/suppliers/feedAdapter.ts` brings in restocks from suppliers. Every 10 minutes it calls the supplier API for new deliveries, converts each delivery into a restock and asks the stock ledger to record it. The adapter is the only module that knows the supplier's data format, so a change on the supplier's side stays inside this one file. A delivery the adapter cannot parse is logged and skipped; it is not retried, because sending the same bad data again would fail the same way.

nodes.stableKey: Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Client and presentation ⨁ Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › API and orchestration ⨁ Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase~f13aa14f~ory service: a tour of the codebase › Observability and error handling § shape#4

Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Client and presentation ⨁ Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › API and orchestration ⨁ Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase~a36a4022~tory service: a tour of the codebase › Observability and error handling § text#7

content.markdown: Postgres holds the ledger entries and the current stock level per warehouse and product; it is the source of truth for stock. Redis holds cached price lists and nothing that cannot be rebuilt from the supplier feed. The message broker carries StockReserved events to other services, such as fulfilment, and also hosts the dead-letter queue described below. Postgres schema changes live in `db/migrations/` and run on every deploy. The supplier API is run by the suppliers, outside our control, and is the only external system Shelfwise calls.

nodes.stableKey: Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Client and presentation ⨁ Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › API and orchestration ⨁ Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase~f03a9fbc~ory service: a tour of the codebase › Observability and error handling § shape#5

content.markdown: Every module logs through the structured logger in `src/platform/log.ts`, which writes one JSON line per event and always includes the correlation ID that the HTTP handlers attached. The handlers log each request, and the retry helper logs each failed attempt.

nodes.title: Codebase Overview
nodes.stableKey: Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Client and presentation ⨁ Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › API and orchestration ⨁ Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase~4f33cd13~ory service: a tour of the codebase › Observability and error handling § text#11

content.markdown: The codebase is structured into distinct layers, with dependencies flowing inwards from the client/API to domain services and persistence. Key components include the Admin UI, API handlers, a reservation orchestrator, and core domain services for stock and pricing. External integrations and robust error handling are also central to the design.

nodes.stableKey: Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Dependency rules § group#0

content.label: Dependency rules
content.takeaway: Three rules govern dependencies to maintain a readable and modular structure.

nodes.title: Domain Modules and HTTP Layer
nodes.stableKey: Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Dependency rules § text#0

content.markdown:
- Nothing in the domain modules may depend on the HTTP layer.
- The ledger and the pricing rules must stay usable from a script or a test without a web server.

nodes.title: Stock Writes to Postgres
nodes.stableKey: Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Dependency rules § text#1

content.markdown:
- Only the ledger writes stock to Postgres.
- The orchestrator and the adapter go through the ledger for stock writes.

nodes.title: Supplier API Calls
nodes.stableKey: Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Dependency rules § text#2

content.markdown: - Only the supplier feed adapter calls the supplier API.

nodes.title: Commonality, Differences, and Importance
nodes.stableKey: Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Dependency rules § text#3

content.markdown: These three rules all define strict dependency boundaries within the system. They differ in the specific layers or components they address: the first focuses on the separation of domain logic from the HTTP layer, the second on centralized database writes for stock, and the third on isolating external API calls. The most critical rule is arguably the first, as it ensures the core business logic (ledger, pricing) remains independent and reusable, preventing tight coupling to the web interface.

content.markdown: Three rules keep the structure readable.

nodes.stableKey: Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Known gaps § group#0

content.label: Known gaps
content.takeaway: Key gaps exist in testing, load handling, and alerting.

nodes.title: Admin UI Automated Tests
nodes.stableKey: Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Known gaps § text#0

content.markdown: - The admin UI has no automated tests yet.

nodes.title: Stock Consistency Under Load
nodes.stableKey: Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Known gaps § text#1

content.markdown:
- The reservation orchestrator and the feed adapter can both change the same product's stock at once.
- The ledger currently relies on a database row lock to keep them consistent.
- Whether that holds under peak load has not been measured.

nodes.title: Dead-Lettered Deliveries Alerting
nodes.stableKey: Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Known gaps § text#2

content.markdown:
- Dead-lettered deliveries are only found when someone opens the admin UI.
- Nothing alerts the team when `inventory.dlq` starts to fill up.

nodes.title: Summary of Gaps
nodes.stableKey: Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Known gaps § text#3

content.markdown: The known gaps highlight areas of missing automation and untested scalability, particularly concerning data consistency and operational visibility.

nodes.stableKey: Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Where to start reading § group#0

content.label: Where to start reading
content.takeaway: Start with `src/orders/reserve.ts` then `src/ledger/ledger.ts` for new contributors.

nodes.stableKey: Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Where to start reading § text#0

content.markdown: New contributors usually start with `src/orders/reserve.ts`, because it shows a whole reservation in about 120 lines and names every module it depends on. After that, `src/ledger/ledger.ts` explains how stock is counted. Each module keeps its tests next to its code.

nodes.title: Main Point
nodes.stableKey: Shelfwise inventory service: a tour of the codebase › Where to start reading § text#1

content.markdown: The recommended starting point for new contributors is `src/orders/reserve.ts`.
